writing.explanation:
`Option` says a value may be absent and that is unremarkable. `Result` says an operation failed and carries why. Converting between them is routine — ok_or turns absence into an error when the caller does need a reason.

Choose the enum according to the decision the caller must make. `Option<T>` represents an ordinary absence: a lookup may find no element. `Result<T, E>` represents a success or a failure whose reason is useful: parsing text can fail because the input is malformed. These meanings affect error messages, retries, and control flow. `unwrap()` removes the branch by panicking when the other variant appears, so it is a poor default at a user-input boundary.

Give a layered example. A cache lookup can return `Option<Value>`. If a missing key is normal, the caller may supply a default. If a required key is absent, the caller can use `ok_or_else` to turn `None` into a domain error. A database lookup can return `Result<Option<Value>, DbError>` because 'not found' and 'database unavailable' are different outcomes. Collapsing both to `None` hides the operational failure.

For an interview answer, describe the successful type and each alternative with a real caller action. Match when the current layer can recover; use `?` to propagate an error when a higher layer owns the decision. Add context at the boundary where you know which operation failed. Avoid saying `Result` is always better because it carries more information. Extra information is useful only when the domain actually has a failure to explain.

If a caller needs both absence and a possible infrastructure failure, `Result<Option<T>, E>` can be clearer than inventing a sentinel error. Explain which layer turns `None` into an error, if any.

Interview follow-up: How would Result<Option<T>, E> distinguish absence from failure? Explain how transpose changes the nesting.
